claim: Walking through an environment generates retinal motion, which humans rely on to perform a variety of visual tasks.
source: Walking through an environment generates retinal motion, which humans rely on to perform a variety of visual tasks.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about vision and locomotion.

claim: Retinal motion patterns are determined by an interconnected set of factors, including gaze location, gaze stabilization, the structure of the environment, and the walker's goals.
source: Retinal motion patterns are determined by an interconnected set of factors, including gaze location, gaze stabilization, the structure of the environment, and the walker's goals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental design and data analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: There are no empirical in situ measurements of how combined eye and body movements interact with real 3D environments to shape the statistics of retinal motion signals prior to this study.
source: However, to date, there are no empirical in situ measurements of how combined eye and body movements interact with real 3D environments to shape the statistics of retinal motion signals.
evidence: This is a claim about the state of the literature, which would be supported by the authors' review of existing research.

claim: Optic flow is commonly referred to as the pattern of motion generated by a moving observer traveling through a stationary environment.
source: A moving observer traveling through a stationary environment generates a pattern of motion that is commonly referred to as optic flow (Gibson, 1950; Koenderink, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational work by Gibson and Koenderink.

claim: Optic flow is often thought of as a simple pattern of expansive motion centered on the direction of heading.
source: While optic flow is often thought of as a simple pattern of expansive motion centered on the direction of heading, this will be true for the retinal motion pattern only in the case of linear motion with gaze centered on heading direction, a condition only rarely met in natural behavior.
evidence: This is a statement about common understanding in the field, supported by established knowledge.

claim: The simple expansive optic flow pattern is only true for linear motion with gaze centered on heading direction, a condition rarely met in natural behavior.
source: While optic flow is often thought of as a simple pattern of expansive motion centered on the direction of heading, this will be true for the retinal motion pattern only in the case of linear motion with gaze centered on heading direction, a condition only rarely met in natural behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by the empirical observations presented in the study.

claim: The actual retinal motion pattern depends on both the three-dimensional structure of the environment and the motion of the eye through space.
source: The actual retinal motion pattern is much more complex and depends on both the three-dimensional structure of the environment and the motion of the eye through space, which in turn depends on the location of the point of gaze in the scene and the gait-induced oscillations of the body.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental measurements and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The pervasive presence of self-motion makes it likely that the structure of motion processing systems is shaped by these patterns at both evolutionary and developmental timescales.
source: The pervasive presence of self-motion makes it likely that the structure of motion processing systems is shaped by these patterns at both evolutionary and developmental timescales.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the implications of the findings for neural organization.

claim: An understanding of the retinal images resulting from binocular viewing geometry allows a better understanding of the way that cortical neurons might encode the 3D environment.
source: A similar point was made by Bonnen et al., 2020, who demonstrated that an understanding of the retinal images resulting from binocular viewing geometry allowed a better understanding of the way that cortical neurons might encode the 3D environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bonnen et al., 2020.

claim: Previous studies using cameras moving through natural environments do not accurately reflect the patterns incident on the human retinae because the movement of the cameras does not mimic the movements of the head, nor does it take into account the location of gaze.
source: A number of studies have examined motion patterns generated by cameras moving through natural environments (Betsch et al., 2005; Zanker and Zeil, 2005), but these data do not accurately reflect the patterns incident on the human retinae because the movement of the cameras does not mimic the movements of the head, nor does it take into account the location of gaze.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and logical inference about the limitations of previous methods.

claim: In natural locomotion, walkers gaze at different locations depending on the complexity of the terrain and the consequent need to find stable footholds.
source: In natural locomotion, walkers gaze at different locations depending on the complexity of the terrain and the consequent need to find stable footholds (Matthis et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Matthis et al., 2018 and by data presented in the current manuscript.

claim: Task goals indirectly affect the motion input during natural locomotion.
source: Thus, task goals indirectly affect the motion input.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between terrain complexity, gaze behavior, and retinal motion.

claim: Natural locomotion is not linear; instead, the head moves through a complex trajectory in space during the gait cycle.
source: In addition, natural locomotion is not linear. Instead, the head moves through a complex trajectory in space during the gait cycle, while the point of gaze remains stable in the environment, and this imparts a complex pattern of rotation and expansion on the retinal flow as recently described by Matthis et al., 2021.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Matthis et al., 2021 and by the data collected in this study.

claim: Retinal motion is generated by the compensatory rotations of the eye in space while the body moves forward during a step, and gaze is held at a fixed location in space.
source: Retinal motion is generated by the compensatory rotations of the eye in space while the body moves forward during a step, and gaze is held at a fixed location in space.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental observations and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Previous work by Calow and Lappe simulated retinal flow patterns using estimates of gaze location and gait oscillations, together with a database of depth images.
source: Previous work on the statistics of retinal motion by Calow and Lappe simulated retinal flow patterns using estimates of gaze location and gait oscillations, together with a database of depth images (Calow and Lappe, 2007; Calow and Lappe, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Calow and Lappe's work.

claim: The in situ data collection strategy used in this study allows measurement of how gaze location varies with terrain, consequently allowing a more precise and realistic evaluation of the natural statistics than in previous studies.
source: However, since terrain is a profound influence on gaze deployment, the in situ data collection strategy we use here allows measurement of how gaze location varies with terrain, consequently allowing a more precise and realistic evaluation of the natural statistics than in previous studies.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantages of the current methodology compared to previous approaches.

claim: A stereotyped pattern of gaze behavior emerges due to the constraints of the task.
source: We find a stereotyped pattern of gaze behavior that emerges due to the constraints of the task, and this pattern of gaze, together with gait-induced head movements, drives much of the variation in the resulting visual motion patterns.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis showing consistent gaze patterns across subjects and terrains.

claim: The pattern of gaze, together with gait-induced head movements, drives much of the variation in the resulting visual motion patterns.
source: We find a stereotyped pattern of gaze behavior that emerges due to the constraints of the task, and this pattern of gaze, together with gait-induced head movements, drives much of the variation in the resulting visual motion patterns.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Walkers stabilize gaze location in the world during locomotion.
source: Most importantly, because walkers stabilize gaze location in the world, the motion statistics result from the motion of the eye in space as it is carried forward by the body while counter-rotating to maintain stability.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental measurements of eye movements during locomotion.

claim: The motion statistics result from the motion of the eye in space as it is carried forward by the body while counter-rotating to maintain stability.
source: Most importantly, because walkers stabilize gaze location in the world, the motion statistics result from the motion of the eye in space as it is carried forward by the body while counter-rotating to maintain stability.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of eye movements and retinal motion patterns.

claim: Eye movements were recorded at 120 Hz.
source: Eye movements were recorded at 120 Hz.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the data collection.

claim: The scene camera recorded at 30 Hz with 1920 × 1080 pixel resolution and 100 deg diagonal field of view.
source: The scene camera recorded at 30 Hz with 1920 × 1080 pixel resolution and 100 deg diagonal field of view.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the data collection.

claim: The Shadow motion capture system recorded at 100 Hz and was used to estimate joint positions and orientations of a full 3D skeleton.
source: The Shadow motion capture system recorded at 100 Hz and was used to estimate joint positions and orientations of a full 3D skeleton.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the data collection.

claim: Participants walked over a range of terrains two times in each direction.
source: Participants walked over a range of terrains two times in each direction.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental procedure.

claim: When the terrain is complex, subjects mostly direct gaze toward the ground a few steps ahead.
source: When the terrain is complex, subjects mostly direct gaze toward the ground a few steps ahead (Matthis et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Matthis et al., 2018 and by data presented in the current manuscript.

claim: Following each saccade, gaze location is held approximately stable in the scene for periods of 200–300 ms so that visual information about upcoming foothold locations can be acquired while the subject moves forward during a step.
source: Following each saccade, gaze location is held approximately stable in the scene for periods of 200–300 ms so that visual information about upcoming foothold locations can be acquired while the subject moves forward during a step.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of eye movement data presented in the manuscript.

claim: While the walker is fixating and holding gaze stable at a particular location on the ground, the eye rotates slowly to offset the forward motion of the body.
source: While the walker is fixating and holding gaze stable at a particular location on the ground, the eye rotates slowly to offset the forward motion of the body.
evidence: This claim is supported by the eye movement data and analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Stabilization is most likely accomplished by the vestibular-ocular reflex, although other eye movement systems might also be involved.
source: Stabilization is most likely accomplished by the vestibular-ocular reflex, although other eye movement systems might also be involved.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of eye movement systems and the characteristics of the observed stabilization.

claim: Saccades were detected based on both horizontal and vertical velocity and acceleration using a velocity threshold of 65 deg/s and an acceleration threshold of 5 deg/s2.
source: We segmented the image into saccades and fixations using an eye-in-orbit velocity threshold of 65 deg/s and an acceleration threshold of 5 deg/s2.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the data analysis.

claim: Retinal image slippage during fixations had a mode of 0.26 deg and a median of 0.83 deg.
source: Retinal image slippage during fixations had a mode of 0.26 deg and a median of 0.83 deg.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of gaze stabilization presented in the Methods section and Figure 10.

claim: There is variation in how far ahead subjects direct gaze between terrain types.
source: There is variation in how far ahead subjects direct gaze between terrain types, as has been observed previously (Matthis et al., 2018), although the pattern of saccades followed by stabilizing eye movements is conserved.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 2 and by citation to Matthis et al., 2018.

claim: The pattern of saccades followed by stabilizing eye movements is conserved across terrain types.
source: There is variation in how far ahead subjects direct gaze between terrain types, as has been observed previously (Matthis et al., 2018), although the pattern of saccades followed by stabilizing eye movements is conserved.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of eye movement patterns across different terrains.

claim: The median gaze angle in rocky terrain is approximately 45 deg, about 2–3 steps ahead.
source: Consistent with previous observations, gaze location is moved closer to the body in the more complex terrains, with the median gaze angle in rocky terrain being approximately 45 deg, about 2–3 steps ahead, and that on pavement being to far distances, a little below the horizontal.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The median gaze angle on pavement is to far distances, a little below the horizontal.
source: Consistent with previous observations, gaze location is moved closer to the body in the more complex terrains, with the median gaze angle in rocky terrain being approximately 45 deg, about 2–3 steps ahead, and that on pavement being to far distances, a little below the horizontal.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The bimodality of most of the gaze angle distributions reflects the observation that subjects alternate between near and far viewing, presumably for different purposes.
source: The bimodality of most of the distributions reflects the observation that subjects alternate between near and far viewing, presumably for different purposes (e.g. path planning versus foothold finding).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed distribution patterns and knowledge of locomotor behavior.

claim: Changes in gaze angle, in conjunction with the movements of the head, have an important effect on retinal motion speeds.
source: These changes in gaze angle, in conjunction with the movements of the head, have an important effect on retinal motion speeds, as will be shown below.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Motion input indirectly stems from behavioral goals.
source: Thus, motion input indirectly stems from behavioral goals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between terrain, gaze behavior, and retinal motion.

claim: Stabilizing eye movements are primarily downward as the body moves forward.
source: Rotations are primarily downward as the body moves forward, with rightward and leftward components resulting from both body sway and fixations to the left or right of the future path, occasioned by the need to change direction or navigate around an obstacle.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 3b.

claim: There are rightward and leftward components of eye movements resulting from both body sway and fixations to the left or right of the future path.
source: Rotations are primarily downward as the body moves forward, with rightward and leftward components resulting from both body sway and fixations to the left or right of the future path, occasioned by the need to change direction or navigate around an obstacle.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 3b.

claim: There are a small number of upward eye movements resulting from vertical gait-related motion of the head, and possibly some small saccades that were misclassified as fixations.
source: There are a small number of upward eye movements resulting from vertical gait-related motion of the head, and possibly some small saccades that were misclassified as fixations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data and knowledge of potential sources of error.

claim: A photogrammetry package called Meshroom was used to estimate a 3D triangle mesh representation of the terrain structure.
source: In order to approximate retinal motion input to the visual system, we first use a photogrammetry package called Meshroom to estimate a 3D triangle mesh representation of the terrain structure, as well as a 3D trajectory through the terrain using the head camera video images.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the data processing.

claim: The mean flow fields for speed and direction were averaged across subjects for all terrains.
source: The mean flow fields for speed and direction, averaged across subjects, for all terrains, are shown in Figure 4.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis and presentation.

claim: Average speeds in the lower visual field peak at approximately 28.8 deg/s at 45 deg eccentricity.
source: Average speeds in the lower visual field peak at approximately 28.8 deg/s (at 45 deg eccentricity), whereas the upper peaks at 13.6 deg/s.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Average speeds in the upper visual field peak at 13.6 deg/s.
source: Average speeds in the lower visual field peak at approximately 28.8 deg/s (at 45 deg eccentricity), whereas the upper peaks at 13.6 deg/s.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The average directions of flow exhibit a radially expansive pattern as expected from the viewing geometry.
source: The average directions of flow exhibit a radially expansive pattern as expected from the viewing geometry.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 4c and by geometric principles.

claim: The expansive motion is not radially symmetric; directions are biased toward the vertical.
source: However, the expansive motion (directly away from center) is not radially symmetric. Directions are biased toward the vertical, with only a narrow band in the left and right visual field exhibiting leftward or rightward motion.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 4c and 4d.

claim: As gaze is directed more toward the horizon, the pattern of increasing speed as a function of eccentricity becomes more radially asymmetric.
source: As gaze is directed more toward the horizon, the pattern of increasing speed as a function of eccentricity becomes more radially asymmetric, with the peak velocity ranging from less than 5 deg/s in the upper visual field to speeds in the range of 20–40 deg/s in the lower visual fields.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: As gaze is lowered to the ground, the peaks in speed move closer together, the variance of the distributions increase in the upper/left/right fields, and the distribution of motion speeds becomes more radially symmetric.
source: As gaze is lowered to the ground, these peaks move closer together, the variance of the distributions increase in the upper/left/right fields, and the distribution of motion speeds becomes more radially symmetric.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Horizontal gaze angle is defined relative to the direction of travel.
source: Horizontal gaze angle is defined relative to the direction of travel.
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the analysis.

claim: Body sway accounts for about ±12 deg of rotation of the eye in the orbit.
source: Body sway accounts for about ±12 deg of rotation of the eye in the orbit.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of body and eye movements.

claim: Fixations to the right and left of the travel path deviate by about ±30 deg of visual angle.
source: Fixations to the right and left of the travel path deviate by about ±30 deg of visual angle.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of gaze behavior.

claim: Changes in horizontal angle primarily influence the spatial pattern of motion direction.
source: Changes in horizontal angle primarily influence the spatial pattern of motion direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Rightward or leftward gaze introduces clockwise or counterclockwise rotation in addition to expansion.
source: This can be seen in the right side of Figure 6 (in c and d), where rightward or leftward gaze introduces clockwise or counterclockwise rotation in addition to expansion.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The added motion from the rocky terrain structure attenuated the speed difference between upper and lower visual fields.
source: Thus, the added motion from the rocky terrain structure attenuated the speed difference between upper and lower visual fields, but otherwise did not affect the distributions very much.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 7.

claim: There is little effect of terrain on the motion direction distributions.
source: There is little effect on the motion direction distributions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 7.

claim: The direction and speed of the motion vectors resulting from local depth variations are likely to average out over the course of the path.
source: This might be expected as the direction and speed of the motion vectors resulting from local depth variations are likely to average out over the course of the path.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data and geometric principles.

claim: Asymmetry between upper and lower visual fields is observed in retinal motion statistics.
source: In these retinal motion statistics, we observe asymmetry between upper and lower visual fields, low velocities at the fovea, speeds less than 20–30 deg/s in the central 90 deg (see Figure 4b), the compression of directions near the horizontal meridian (see Figure 4c), the preponderance of vertical directions (see Figure 4d), modulated by lateral gaze positions (see Figure 6d), resulting in global rotational patterns (see Figure 6c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Low velocities at the fovea are observed in retinal motion statistics.
source: In these retinal motion statistics, we observe asymmetry between upper and lower visual fields, low velocities at the fovea, speeds less than 20–30 deg/s in the central 90 deg (see Figure 4b), the compression of directions near the horizontal meridian (see Figure 4c), the preponderance of vertical directions (see Figure 4d), modulated by lateral gaze positions (see Figure 6d), resulting in global rotational patterns (see Figure 6c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Speeds are less than 20–30 deg/s in the central 90 deg of the visual field.
source: In these retinal motion statistics, we observe asymmetry between upper and lower visual fields, low velocities at the fovea, speeds less than 20–30 deg/s in the central 90 deg (see Figure 4b), the compression of directions near the horizontal meridian (see Figure 4c), the preponderance of vertical directions (see Figure 4d), modulated by lateral gaze positions (see Figure 6d), resulting in global rotational patterns (see Figure 6c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 4b.

claim: There is compression of directions near the horizontal meridian.
source: In these retinal motion statistics, we observe asymmetry between upper and lower visual fields, low velocities at the fovea, speeds less than 20–30 deg/s in the central 90 deg (see Figure 4b), the compression of directions near the horizontal meridian (see Figure 4c), the preponderance of vertical directions (see Figure 4d), modulated by lateral gaze positions (see Figure 6d), resulting in global rotational patterns (see Figure 6c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 4c.

claim: There is a preponderance of vertical directions in retinal motion.
source: In these retinal motion statistics, we observe asymmetry between upper and lower visual fields, low velocities at the fovea, speeds less than 20–30 deg/s in the central 90 deg (see Figure 4b), the compression of directions near the horizontal meridian (see Figure 4c), the preponderance of vertical directions (see Figure 4d), modulated by lateral gaze positions (see Figure 6d), resulting in global rotational patterns (see Figure 6c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 4d.

claim: Lateral gaze positions modulate the preponderance of vertical directions, resulting in global rotational patterns.
source: In these retinal motion statistics, we observe asymmetry between upper and lower visual fields, low velocities at the fovea, speeds less than 20–30 deg/s in the central 90 deg (see Figure 4b), the compression of directions near the horizontal meridian (see Figure 4c), the preponderance of vertical directions (see Figure 4d), modulated by lateral gaze positions (see Figure 6d), resulting in global rotational patterns (see Figure 6c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figures 6c and 6d.

claim: This work does not sample the broad domain of motion input and pertains only to the case of locomotion in the presence of a ground plane.
source: Note that this work does not (and does not intend to) sample the broad domain of motion input and pertains only to the case of locomotion in the presence of a ground plane.
evidence: This is a statement about the scope and limitations of the study.

claim: The results do not pertain to eye movement patterns involving smooth pursuit of a moving target or optokinetic nystagmus.
source: Nor do the results pertain to eye movement patterns involving smooth pursuit of a moving target or optokinetic nystagmus.
evidence: This is a statement about the scope and limitations of the study.

claim: Many of the features of the retinal motion distributions stem from a combination of the ground plane, the saccade and fixate strategy, the gait-induced movements of the head, and the task-linked fixation locations.
source: However, many of the features of the retinal motion distributions stem from a combination of the ground plane, the saccade and fixate strategy, the gait-induced movements of the head, and the task-linked fixation locations, so one might expect the present observations would cover a substantial domain of experienced motion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of the factors contributing to retinal motion patterns.

claim: The velocities scale with the ratio of eye height to walking speed.
source: While the geometry will depend on factors such as eye height, the velocities scale with the ratio of eye height to walking speed.
evidence: This is a statement based on geometric principles.

claim: The results are general across a range of normal walking speeds.
source: The results are also general across a range of normal walking speeds.
evidence: This is a claim about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: The ubiquitous pattern of very low velocities at the fovea is expected from the pervasive stabilization of gaze.
source: Perhaps the most notable feature of the retinal motion is the ubiquitous pattern of very low velocities at the fovea, as expected from the pervasive stabilization of gaze.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data and by knowledge of gaze stabilization mechanisms.

claim: The flow field is reminiscent of Gibson's formulation of optic flow, with the focus of expansion centered at the point of gaze.
source: While the flow field is reminiscent of Gibson's formulation of optic flow (Gibson, 1950), with the focus of expansion centered at the point of gaze, the context is very different from the one Gibson first described, resulting from active stabilization rather than coincidence of gaze with the direction of travel (Matthis et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with Gibson's work and by citation to Matthis et al., 2021.

claim: The context of the observed flow field is very different from the one Gibson first described, resulting from active stabilization rather than coincidence of gaze with the direction of travel.
source: While the flow field is reminiscent of Gibson's formulation of optic flow (Gibson, 1950), with the focus of expansion centered at the point of gaze, the context is very different from the one Gibson first described, resulting from active stabilization rather than coincidence of gaze with the direction of travel (Matthis et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data and by citation to Matthis et al., 2021.

claim: Flow patterns from self-motion are generated only indirectly from body motion.
source: Flow patterns from self-motion are generated only indirectly from body motion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of how retinal motion is generated during gaze stabilization.

claim: The retinal motion pattern stems from counter-rotation of the eye in the orbit to keep gaze location stable in the world, in response to the variation in momentary translation and rotation of the head during the gait cycle.
source: The retinal motion pattern (with low velocities at the fovea) all stems from counter-rotation of the eye in the orbit to keep gaze location stable in the world, in response to the variation in momentary translation and rotation of the head during the gait cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of eye and body movements.

claim: Head-relative flow is a poor signal to guide locomotor direction.
source: This variation in momentary head direction makes head-relative flow a poor signal to guide locomotor direction, as discussed by Matthis et al., 2021, who suggest that instead retinal flow patterns are used for control of balance while stepping.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Matthis et al., 2021 and by inference from the data.

claim: Retinal flow patterns are used for control of balance while stepping.
source: This variation in momentary head direction makes head-relative flow a poor signal to guide locomotor direction, as discussed by Matthis et al., 2021, who suggest that instead retinal flow patterns are used for control of balance while stepping.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Matthis et al., 2021.

claim: Calow and Lappe estimated that the gain of the stabilizing rotations was Gaussian with a mean and standard deviation of 0.5 based on pursuit and optokinetic movements.
source: In a previous attempt to capture these statistics, Calow and Lappe, 2007; Calow and Lappe, 2008 also found generally low velocities at the fovea, but they estimated that the gain of the stabilizing rotations was Gaussian with a mean and standard deviation of 0.5 based on pursuit and optokinetic movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Calow and Lappe's work.

claim: The Vestibular Ocular Reflex (VOR) is likely the primary source of the stabilizing movements given its low latency and the increase in VOR gain during locomotion associated with spinal modulation.
source: It seems likely that the Vestibular Ocular Reflex (VOR) is the primary source of the stabilizing movements given its low latency and the increase in VOR gain during locomotion associated with spinal modulation (Dietrich and Wuehr, 2019; Haggerty and King, 2018; MacNeilage et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and by knowledge of eye movement systems.

claim: Calow and Lappe's assumption of low stabilization gain introduces added motion at the fovea and throughout the visual field.
source: Calow and Lappe's assumption of low stabilization gain introduces added motion at the fovea and throughout the visual field.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with Calow and Lappe's methodology.

claim: Measurements in this study and previous ones indicate that gain in real-world conditions is much closer to unity (1.0), with only modest retinal slip during fixations.
source: Our measurements, and previous ones (Imai et al., 2001; Authié et al., 2015), indicate that gain in real-world conditions is much closer to unity (1.0), with only modest retinal slip during fixations (10).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript and by citations to previous work.

claim: Given the ubiquitous nature of stabilizing behavior and the pervasive presence of head movements in natural behavior, the low velocities in the central visual field should be the norm.
source: Given the ubiquitous nature of this kind of stabilizing behavior and the pervasive presence of head movements in natural behavior, the low velocities in the central visual field should be the norm (Land, 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and supported by citation to Land, 2019.

claim: The low velocities in the central visual field support the assumption of a motion prior centered on zero, proposed by Weiss et al., 2002.
source: This result supports the assumption of a motion prior centered on zero, proposed by Weiss et al., 2002, in order to account for particular motion illusions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Weiss et al., 2002 and by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A strong asymmetry in retinal motion speed between the upper and lower visual fields was observed.
source: We observed a strong asymmetry in retinal motion speed between the upper and lower visual fields (see Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 4c.

claim: The asymmetry between upper and lower visual fields is stronger for optic flow during gaze ahead (gaze angle of 60–90 deg) compared to when participants direct their gaze lower in their visual field (gaze angle of 17–45 deg).
source: Further analysis of the modulation due to gaze angle reveals that this asymmetry is stronger for optic flow during gaze ahead (gaze angle of 60–90 deg, see top panel in Figure 5b) compared to when participants direct their gaze lower in their visual field (gaze angle of 17–45 deg, see lower panel in Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 5b.

claim: The asymmetry between upper and lower visual fields was also observed by Calow and Lappe, 2007 and Calow and Lappe, 2008.
source: The asymmetry between upper and lower visual fields was also observed by Calow and Lappe, 2007 and Calow and Lappe, 2008 (in particular, see Figure 2 from Calow and Lappe, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Calow and Lappe's work.

claim: Calow and Lappe concluded that asymmetries in flow are driven primarily by the asymmetries in depth statistics.
source: They concluded that these asymmetries in flow are driven primarily by the asymmetries in depth statistics. Our findings agree with this conclusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Calow and Lappe's work and by the data in the current manuscript.

claim: When the gaze is lower (17–45 deg), the depth statistics become more uniform between the upper and lower visual field, resulting in a much smaller difference between the retinal motion speeds in the upper vs. lower visual field.
source: When the gaze is lower (17–45 deg; see lower panel of Figure 5b), the depth statistics become more uniform between the upper and lower visual field, resulting in a much smaller difference between the retinal motion speeds in the upper vs. lower visual field.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 5b.

claim: In Calow and Lappe, 2007, they relied on a gaze distribution that was not linked to the visual demands of locomotion.
source: In Calow and Lappe, 2007, they relied on a gaze distribution that was not linked to the visual demands of locomotion, so the entirety of their optic flow statistics were examined for gaze vectors between elevations of 70–110 deg.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology of Calow and Lappe's work.

claim: During visually guided locomotion, participants often lower their gaze to the ground, which dramatically changes the relative depth statistics of the upper/lower visual field, diminishing the field asymmetries.
source: During visually guided locomotion, participants often lower their gaze to the ground. That lowering of gaze dramatically changes the relative depth statistics of the upper/lower visual field, diminishing the field asymmetries.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The difference in gaze distributions and the difference in VOR gain are big drivers of why the retinal motion statistics in this study are somewhat larger in magnitude than those reported in Calow and Lappe, 2007.
source: We also note that this difference in gaze distributions (as well as the difference in VOR gain discussed above) is a big driver of why our retinal motion statistics are somewhat larger in magnitude than those reported in Calow and Lappe, 2007.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with Calow and Lappe's work.

claim: A band of low speeds in the horizontal direction centered on the fovea was found.
